title: Europe’s Ancient Landscapes May Have Been More Open Than We Thought
paragraphs: Many people imagine that Europe was once covered by endless, dark forest. A new study from Aarhus University in Denmark suggests that this picture may be wrong. The researchers combined several kinds of evidence: fossil pollen, plant remains, charcoal from ancient wildfires, chemical traces in the teeth and bones of animals, fossil insects and ancient DNA found in sediments.

According to the team, Europe was mostly a changing mix of trees, open ground and flowering plants for more than 20 million years. This was true in climates similar to today’s, and also in warmer and colder periods. Large plant-eating animals, such as elephants, rhinoceroses, wild cattle and bison, probably kept the landscape open by grazing and disturbing the soil.

The authors argue that this has consequences for modern nature policy, because some reforestation programmes only pay for dense forest. They suggest that mixed habitats and large grazing animals may help biodiversity more. However, this is one review of past evidence, and no single type of evidence tells the whole story. The results appeared in the journal Biological Conservation.
